extracted.intended_audience: ML researchers, conference program chairs, and peer-review policy-makers studying LLM effects on peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing how use of large language models (LLMs) by authors, reviewers, and metareviewers affects review scores, metareview decisions, and paper acceptance in major ML conferences (ICLR/ICML/NeurIPS). Includes detection of LLM use, statistical tests, and synthetic LLM-generated review experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: α value threshold (LLM-aided classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: α value of 0.15 is used as a threshold: Papers and Reviews are classified as LLM-aided if they have α>0.15 and Human otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This threshold is applied consistently across analyses and tables (papers, reviews, metareviews). Metareviews with α>0.15 are treated as LLM-aided in regressions; the 0.15 cutoff drives quadrant assignments in summary statistics tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting LLM use (Liang et al. MLE method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame detection as a Maximum Likelihood Estimation problem: assume text x is drawn from a mixture (1-α)P + αQ, and find α that maximizes ℒ(α)=∑_i log((1-α)P(x_i)+αQ(x_i)). Base distributions P (human) and Q (LLM) are estimated using unigram frequency models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P is estimated from human-written text and Q from LLM-generated paraphrases. The authors use provided pre-computed word frequency distributions trained on CS paper abstracts (arXiv cs.CL and cs.LG) before Nov 2023. Sentences x_i are the unit of observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall Rating (conference-specific scales)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Overall Rating' or 'Rating' field provided by reviewers (used as the primary outcome in many analyses). Scales vary by conference (e.g., ICLR 1–10, NeurIPS 1–6, ICML 1–5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in within-paper paired analyses, synthetic review experiments, and as a predictor (mean rating) in logistic regressions for acceptance. Analyses account for differing scales per conference when reporting CATEs and comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer Confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A numeric 'Confidence' field reviewers must provide alongside ratings (reported in summary statistics and plotted across quality buckets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed trends: both LLM-aided and human reviews show lower confidence for higher-quality papers; human reviews have slightly higher confidence than LLM-aided reviews. Fully LLM-generated reviews often assign a uniform confidence (e.g., 4), suggesting limited calibrated confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review content rating dimensions (Contribution, Soundness, Presentation, Quality, Clarity, Significance, Originality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple per-review rating fields (examples include Contribution, Soundness, Presentation; or Quality, Clarity, Significance, Originality depending on venue) that capture different aspects of paper merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses show similar trends across these fields as for Overall Rating (e.g., LLM-aided reviews give slightly higher scores to low-quality papers). Figures and tables report mean ± std dev for these dimensions by (Paper, Review) quadrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean rating (mean rating)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mean rating captures the central tendency of reviewer scores for a paper; used as a covariate in acceptance models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In logistic regression for acceptance, mean rating strongly predicts acceptance (example coefficient β1=+3.327, p<0.001). Always included when assessing whether LLM assistance in metareviews affects acceptance beyond score information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard deviation of ratings (std rating)
rubrics_metrics.description: Std rating measures disagreement among reviewers (the dispersion of reviewer scores).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher rating variance is associated with lower acceptance probability (example coefficient β2≈−0.288, p<0.001). Used as a control in logistic regression models predicting acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logistic regression for acceptance (Eq. 8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Model: logit(P_accepted) = β1(mean rating) + β2(std rating) + β3 I_metareview + γ' Z, where I_metareview is an indicator for LLM-aided metareviews and Z are area fixed effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The coefficient β3 measures whether LLM-aided metareviews associate with different acceptance probabilities after controlling for mean score, disagreement, and area. Table IX reports β3>0 indicating higher acceptance likelihood for papers with LLM-aided metareviews, controlling for scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Within-paper paired analysis (Δ_i)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each paper compute treatment effects Δ_i using only the non-quality-indicator reviews and test whether Δ_i differs between LLM and human papers; CATE Diff. = mean(Δ_i for LLM papers) − mean(Δ_i for human papers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This within-paper paired approach compares reviewer behavior on the same paper to control for paper quality. Results are tested with Mann–Whitney U tests (one-tailed) and stratified by quality buckets to probe heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mann–Whitney U test (one-tailed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-parametric test used to compare distributions of treatment effects or ratings between groups (applied one-tailed in reported tables).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for within-paper paired analyses (Table VII) and synthetic LLM vs human review comparisons (Table VIII). p-values reported alongside point estimates to indicate statistical significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regression with interaction (Eq. 9) to estimate LLM effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Model: Y_ij = β0 + β1 X_i^{LLM} + β2 T_ij + β3 (X_i^{LLM} × T_ij) + γ' Z_i + ε_ij, where X_i^{LLM} indicates paper was LLM-aided and T_ij indicates review was LLM-aided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: β1 measures average difference for LLM-aided papers, β2 measures effect of LLM-aided reviews on human papers (CATE(Human)=β2), β2+β3 measures effect on LLM-aided papers (CATE(LLM)). Used to demonstrate asymmetric relationships (e.g., LLM-aided reviews help LLM-aided papers more).

rubrics_metrics.name: CATE estimation and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: CATE(Human) = β2; CATE(LLM) = β2 + β3; difference β3 quantifies whether LLM-aided reviews have differential effects when evaluating LLM-aided papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerical examples: in ICLR 2024, β2≈0.271 (LLM-aided reviews increase ratings on human papers), β2+β3≈0.615 on LLM papers, and β3≈0.344 indicates a significantly stronger positive effect when both paper and review are LLM-aided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality buckets defined by left-out human review
rubrics_metrics.description: Paper quality is determined using a left-out human review; remaining human reviews are used to plot the comparison curves and to assign papers to quality buckets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedure creates an out-of-sample quality measure for stratified analyses (Figures 4, 7, 8). It is used to show that LLM-aided review leniency is concentrated in lower quality buckets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of fully LLM-generated reviews (rating compression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fully LLM-generated reviews assign ratings almost exclusively between 6 and 7 regardless of paper quality, exhibiting minimal slope across quality buckets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This compression implies poor discrimination: fully LLM-generated reviews inflate ratings for weak papers and give little signal about merit, undermining peer review accuracy. Human-in-the-loop moderation partially mitigates compression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment and diagnostic metrics for synthetic metareviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Metrics include alignment % between synthetic metareviews and actual decisions, synthetic accept rate, actual accept rate, and precision/recall of synthetic accept recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported example: fully LLM-generated metareviews align with actual decisions 72.6% overall; synthetic accept rate 19.1% vs actual 46.5%. Synthetic accepts achieve 100% precision (when recommending accept the paper was actually accepted) but have low recall (e.g., 43.2% for human metareviews), indicating systematic underprediction of acceptances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of area fixed effects (Z vector) as regression controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Z represents area fixed effects (paper research area indicators) included in regressions to control for confounders; mappings between ICLR 2024 and 2025 area labels are provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including area indicators controls for variation across subfields. The combined dataset uses a mapped set of 23 research areas; significant area coefficients are reported (e.g., learning theory, generative models).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of CATE Diff. for within-paper comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: CATE Diff. = mean(Δ_i for LLM papers) − mean(Δ_i for human papers) as reported in Table VII.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to summarize within-paper paired differences in treatment effects across quality buckets; p-values from Mann–Whitney U tests indicate whether differences are statistically significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling/oversampling strategy for synthetic LLM experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Fully LLM-generated reviews and metareviews were produced for randomly sampled papers with oversampling of LLM-aided papers (to ensure reliable analysis): e.g., sample counts such as 60 LLM-aided and 480 human papers for ICLR 2025, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The oversampling is necessary because LLM-aided papers are a minority in the corpora; analyses and p-values account for these sampling decisions when comparing synthetic LLM judgments to human judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation guidance: differential effects vs compositional heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent LLM–LLM interaction (LLM-aided reviews favoring LLM-aided papers) is driven primarily by compositional overrepresentation of LLM-aided papers in low-quality ranges where LLM-aided reviews are generally lenient, rather than by specific favoritism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This interpretive standard is derived from combining regression, within-paper paired analysis, and quality-bucket stratification: restrict analyses to accepted/high-quality papers to test whether interaction persists (often disappears).
